title: Orange Meringue Pie
summary: A sunny twist on the lemon classic: a tangy fresh orange curd in a crisp shell under a billowing, golden Swiss meringue.
equipment: heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Prepare the pastry
steps.text: Mix the flour, sugar and salt, rub in the butter until it resembles rough breadcrumbs, then add enough iced water to form a soft dough. Wrap and chill for 1 hour.

steps.title: Bake the shell
steps.text: Line the dish with the rolled-out dough, crimp the rim and chill 30 minutes. Bake at 190 °C (170 °C fan) under paper and beans for 20 minutes, then bare for 10-12 minutes until golden. Turn the oven down to 180 °C (160 °C fan).

steps.title: Cook the orange curd
steps.text: Whisk the sugar, cornflour and salt in the saucepan, then whisk in the orange juice, lemon juice and zest. Bring to the boil over a medium heat, whisking, and let it bubble for 1 minute until thick and translucent. Whisk a ladleful into the yolks to warm them, pour back into the pan and cook, still whisking, for 1 minute more (well above 71 °C). Beat in the butter, then pour the hot filling into the baked shell; it needs to be hot when the meringue goes on so the two bond.

steps.title: Make a Swiss meringue
steps.text: Whisk the whites, sugar and cream of tartar in the heatproof bowl over barely simmering water until the sugar dissolves and the mix reaches 71 °C, which makes the whites safe to eat. Take off the heat and beat with the hand mixer for 4-5 minutes, adding the vanilla, until stiff, glossy and cooled.

steps.title: Top and bake
steps.text: Spread the meringue over the hot filling, pushing it right onto the pastry rim to seal so it does not shrink or weep, and pull it up into peaks. Bake 12-15 minutes until the peaks are golden.

steps.title: Cool
steps.text: Let the pie cool on a rack for 1 hour, then chill for about 3 hours so the filling sets cleanly for slicing.

tips: Use freshly squeezed juice; cartons are often too sweet and flat for a curd.
The usual mistake is putting the meringue on a cold filling, which makes it slide and weep. Keep the curd hot.
Clean the bowl and whisk well; even a trace of fat stops the whites from whipping.
For extra colour, brown the peaks briefly with a kitchen blowtorch after baking.
Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Best eaten on the day. Leftovers keep, uncovered, in the fridge for 1 day; the meringue may bead slightly.
